danish.title: Anden epilog — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Nationernes liv er ikke indeholdt i nogle få mænds liv, for forbindelsen mellem disse mænd og nationerne er ikke fundet. Teorien om, at denne forbindelse beror på folkeviljes overførsel til visse historiske personer, er en hypotese, der ikke bekræftes af historiens erfaring.

Teorien om folkeviljes overførsel til historiske personer kan måske forklare meget inden for retsvidenskabens domæne og være nødvendig for dens formål, men i sin anvendelse på historie forklarer den ingenting, så snart revolutioner, erobringer eller borgerkrige indtræffer — det vil sige, så snart historien begynder.
Teorien forekommer uigendrivelig, netop fordi handlingen med at overføre folkeviljen ikke kan efterprøves, da den aldrig har fundet sted.
Uanset hvad der sker, og hvem der end måtte stå i spidsen for tingene, kan teorien altid sige, at den og den person tog ledelsen, fordi den kollektive vilje blev overført til ham.

De svar, denne teori giver på historiske spørgsmål, ligner svarene fra en mand, der betragter en kvæghjords bevægelser og ikke agter på græsgangens skiftende kvalitet i markens forskellige dele eller hyrdens drivning, men tilskriver hjordens retning det dyr, der tilfældigvis befinder sig forrest.

»Hjorden går i den retning, fordi dyret forrest leder den, og den kollektive vilje hos alle de andre dyr er overdraget til denne leder.« Således siger historikerne af den første klasse — dem, der antager den betingelsesløse overførsel af folkeviljen.

»Hvis de dyr, der leder hjorden, skifter, skyldes det, at den kollektive vilje hos alle dyrene overføres fra én leder til en anden, alt efter om dyret fører dem i den retning, hele hjorden har valgt, eller ej.« Sådan svarer historikere, der antager, at den kollektive folkevilje delegeres til herskerne under betingelser, de anser for kendte. (Med denne observationsmetode sker det ofte, at iagttageren, påvirket af den retning, han selv foretrækker, betragter dem som ledere, der på grund af folkets retningsskift ikke længere er forrest, men til siden eller endda bagerst.)

»Hvis dyrene forrest bestandig skifter, og hele hjordens retning bestandig ændres, skyldes det, at dyrene, for at følge en given retning, overfører deres vilje til de dyr, der har tiltrukket vores opmærksomhed, og for at studere hjordens bevægelser må vi iagttage alle de fremtrædende dyrs bevægelser på alle sider af hjorden.« Således siger den tredje klasse af historikere, der betragter alle historiske personer, fra monarker til journalister, som udtryk for deres tid.
Teorien om folkeviljes overførsel til historiske personer er blot en parafrase — en genfortælling af spørgsmålet med andre ord.

Hvad forårsager historiske begivenheder? Magt. Hvad er magt? Magt er folkeviljens overførsel til én person. Under hvilken betingelse delegeres folkeviljen til én person? På betingelse af, at denne person udtrykker hele folkets vilje. Det vil sige: magt er magt: med andre ord er magt et ord, hvis betydning vi ikke forstår.

Hvis menneskekundskabens rige var begrænset til abstrakt ræsonnement, ville menneskeheden, efter at have underkastet retsvidenskabens forklaring af »magt« en kritik, konkludere, at magt blot er et ord og ikke har nogen virkelig eksistens. Men for at forstå fænomener har mennesket, foruden abstrakt ræsonnement, erfaringen, hvormed det efterprøver sine overvejelser. Og erfaringen fortæller os, at magt ikke blot er et ord, men et virkeligt eksisterende fænomen.
For ikke at tale om, at ingen beskrivelse af menneskers kollektive virksomhed kan undvære magtbegrebet, bevises magtens eksistens både af historien og af iagttagelse af samtidige begivenheder.

Hver gang en begivenhed indtræffer, viser der sig en mand eller mænd, ved hvis vilje begivenheden synes at have fundet sted. Napoleon den Tredje udsteder et dekret, og franskmændene drager til Mexico. Preussens konge og Bismarck udsteder dekreter, og en hær rykker ind i Bøhmen. Napoleon den Første udsteder et dekret, og en hær rykker ind i Rusland. Alexander den Første giver en befaling, og franskmændene underkaster sig Bourbonerne. Erfaringen viser os, at hvilken begivenhed der end indtræffer, er den altid forbundet med én eller flere personers vilje, der har forordnet den.

Historikerne vil i overensstemmelse med den gamle vane at anerkende guddommelig indgriben i menneskelige anliggender se begivenhedernes årsag i udtrykkene for en magtbeklædt persons vilje, men denne antagelse bekræftes hverken af fornuften eller af erfaringen.

På den ene side viser tænkningen, at udtrykket for en mands vilje — hans ord — kun er en del af den almene virksomhed, der udtrykkes i en begivenhed, som for eksempel i en krig eller en revolution, og uden at antage en uforståelig, overnaturlig kraft — et mirakel — kan man ikke indrømme, at ord kan være den umiddelbare årsag til millioner af menneskers bevægelser. På den anden side, selv om vi indrømmede, at ord kunne være årsag til begivenheder, viser historien, at de historiske personers viljesudtryk i de fleste tilfælde ikke har nogen virkning, det vil sige, deres befalinger udføres ofte ikke, og undertiden sker det stik modsatte af, hvad de befaler.
Uden at antage guddommelig indgriben i menneskenes anliggender kan vi ikke betragte »magt« som årsag til begivenheder.
Magt er, set fra erfaringens standpunkt, blot det forhold, der eksisterer mellem udtrykket for nogens vilje og udførelsen af denne vilje af andre.
For at forklare betingelserne for dette forhold må vi først opstille et begreb om viljesudtrykket med henvisning til mennesket og ikke til Guddommen.

Hvis Guddommen udsteder en befaling og udtrykker Sin vilje, som oldtidens historie fortæller os, er udtrykket for denne vilje uafhængigt af tiden og forårsages ikke af noget, for Guddommen kontrolleres ikke af en begivenhed. Men taler vi om befalinger, der er udtryk for menneskers vilje, som handler i tid og i forhold til hinanden, må vi, for at forklare forbindelsen mellem befalinger og begivenheder, genoprette: (1) betingelsen for alt, hvad der sker: bevægelsens kontinuitet i tid, både begivenhedernes og den befalende persons, og (2) uundgåeligheden af forbindelsen mellem den befalende person og dem, der udfører hans befaling.

english.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a few men, because the connection between those men and the nations has not been found. The theory that this connection is based on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical persons is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historic persons may explain much in the domain of jurisprudence and may be essential for its purposes; but in its application to history—as soon as revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur, that is, as soon as history actually begins—the theory explains nothing.
The theory seems irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will can never be verified, since it never actually occurred.
Whatever happens and whoever stands at the head of affairs, the theory can always say that such-and-such a person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

The answers this theory gives to historical questions are like the replies of a man who, watching the movements of a herd of cattle and paying no attention to the varying quality of the pasture in different parts of the field, or to the herdsman's driving, attributes the herd's direction to whichever animal happens to be at the front.

"The herd goes in that direction because the animal in front leads it, and the collective will of all the other animals is vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say—those who assume the unconditional transfer of the people's will.

"If the animals at the front of the herd change, this happens because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction chosen by the whole herd." This is the answer given by historians who assume the collective will of the masses is transferred to rulers on certain conditions which they regard as known. (With this method of observation it often happens that the observer, influenced by the direction he himself prefers, regards those as leaders who, owing to the people’s change of direction, are no longer in front, but on one side, or even in the rear.)

"If the animals at the front keep changing and the whole herd keeps shifting direction, this is because—in order to follow a given direction—the animals transfer their will to whichever animal has caught our attention, and so to study the movement of the herd we must observe all the noticeable animals moving on all sides of the herd." So say the third class of historians who consider all historical figures—from monarchs to journalists—as expressions of their time.
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical persons is merely a paraphrase—a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what conditions is the will of the people delegated to one person? On the condition that the person expresses the will of the whole people. That is, power is power. In other words: power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then—having critically examined the explanation of "power" that jurisprudence offers—humanity would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence. But for understanding phenomena, besides abstract reasoning, people have another instrument: experience. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word but an actually existing phenomenon.
Not to mention that no description of collective human activity can do without the concept of power, the existence of power is proved both by history and by observing present-day events.

Whenever an event occurs, a person or persons appear by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and Bismarck issue decrees and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree and an army enters Russia. Alexander I issues a decree and the French submit to the Bourbons. Experience shows us that whenever an event takes place it is connected with the will of one or several people who ordered it.

Historians, following their old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, try to see the cause of events in the expression of the will of someone endowed with power. But this assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a person's will—his words—are only part of the total activity expressed in an event, such as a war or a revolution. And so, without invoking some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words can be the immediate cause of the movement of millions of people. On the other hand, even if we admitted that words can be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of historical figures' wills in most cases produces no effect at all—that is, their orders are often not carried out, and sometimes the very opposite of what they commanded takes place.
Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot regard "power" as the cause of events.
Power, from the standpoint of experience, is merely the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.
To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a concept of the expression of will, referring it to man and not to God.

If God gives a command, expressing His will as the ancient histories tell us, that expression of will stands outside time and nothing causes it, for no event governs the Deity. Human beings, on the other hand, issue commands in time and in relation to one another. To explain how their commands connect with events, we must bring two things back into the account. First, the condition of everything that happens: both events and the person giving the orders move continuously through time. Second, the necessary connection between the person giving an order and those who carry it out.
